name: Uchumataqu
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Hannß, Katja. 2008. Uchumataqu: The lost language of the Urus of Bolivia. A grammatical description of the language as documented between 1894 and 1952. Leiden: CNWS Publications (Indigenous Languages of Latin America 7); PhD dissertation, Radboud Universiteit Nijmegen. Open-access publisher's version, Radboud repository hdl:2066/68277 (saved from the Internet Archive snapshot of the repository PDF).
catalog_locator: Chapter 2 Phonology, §2.13.2 'Stress', pp. 117-123; supporting statements p. 3 Introduction, §2.14 p. 123, and the areal-features paragraph of the contact section (p. 10).
catalog_quote: 2.13.2 Stress. Main word stress in morphologically simple forms lies on the penultimate syllable, as already observed by Uhle (1894:2). Stress is indicated by an acute <'>, as in: (212) pá.ya 'adobe brick' (Lehmann 1929b:1); hí.pu 'wind' (Vellard 1949:162); čé.ra 'hair' (Uhle 1894:64.2); á.ča 'head' (Vellard 1950:57). Even in the case of inflection, stress remains on the penultimate syllable, as demonstrated in example (213), in which stressed elements are marked bold. [...] Although in example (213) stress mostly falls on the penultimate syllable, there are irregularities since e.g. katá-šráp'a is doubly stressed. In what follows, I will present changes that take place when morphologically simple forms undergo affixation. It is important to point out that the data do not provide rules governing the distribution but rather tendencies and that there are counterexamples to the claims presented below. This is probably due to obsolescene phenomena in the process of language extinction. The situation is further complicated by the fact that stress is not always marked consistently. Within a single source, some words may be marked for stress while others not. Polo (1901) and Métraux (1935) do not indicate stress at all. (p. 117)
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: In morphologically simple words main stress falls on the penultimate syllable (Hannß, citing Uhle 1894). Under affixation the archival data show only tendencies: stress may stay on the old penult, shift to the new penult, or the word may carry double/triple stress; final stress is exceptional and emphatic; verbal stress is too variable to state rules. Hannß therefore treats penultimate stress as a tendency rather than an exceptionless rule (p. 3: 'a tendency to place stress on the penultimate syllable, although this is not compulsory') and does not mark stress elsewhere in the grammar (p. 123).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress as such; Hannß describes 'double' and 'triple' stress: a monosyllabic nominal stem plus a bisyllabic suffix receives double stress (e.g. hux'-kama), most trisyllabic nominal stems already bear alternating double stress with the first syllable stressed (p. 119), and verbs optionally take a second stress on the 1sg markers -u/-a or in-group -acu (p. 121).
new_statements.exceptions: Bisyllabic stem + bisyllabic suffix and mono-/bisyllabic verbs with 1sg -u/-a (p. 3); monosyllabic stem + monosyllabic suffix keeps stress in situ, so it is often not the penult (p. 118); monosyllabic verb stems with a monosyllabic suffix tend to shift stress to the final syllable, e.g. imperative ondí (p. 122); stress on the final syllable is exceptional and emphatic; declarative -cay is always unstressed (p. 120); purposive -srap'a keeps stress on its own first syllable (p. 122-123); stress marking is inconsistent within sources and Polo (1901) and Métraux (1935) mark no stress at all (p. 117).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in a dormant language reconstructed from archival transcriptions (Uhle 1894, Polo 1901, Lehmann 1929, Métraux 1935, Vellard 1949-1967), not from fieldwork; examples are cited forms and text words from those sources; Hannß calls the patterns tendencies, not rules.
new_statements.identity_note: Hannß 2008 describes Uchumataqu, the Uru of Irohito (Iru-Itu / Ancoaqui) on the Desaguadero, Bolivia, as recorded 1894-1952; Glottolog lists Uchumataqu, Iro-Itu and Uro as alternate names of uruu1244, so the identity matches. It is not Chipaya (chip1262), and it is distinct from the Uru of Ch'imu / Puno bay (Peru) treated by Hannß 2014 and Cerrón-Palomino et al. 2016, which Glottolog also files under uruu1244. Hannß's stress data come from archival transcriptions (chiefly Vellard 1949-67, Uhle 1894, Lehmann 1929), not fieldwork, and she calls the penultimate pattern a tendency with many exceptions under affixation.

tone.quote: Con tales restricciones fonotácticas, la estructura silábica, en verdad muy simple, podía resumirse en la fórmula (C)V(C). Por lo que toca al acento de intensidad, éste ocupaba una posición fija, localizada en la penúltima sílaba. En lo que sigue nos ocuparemos de las consonantes postuladas, presentándolas en series, con los cognados que sustentan su reconstrucción.
tone.translation: With such phonotactic restrictions, the syllable structure, in truth very simple, could be summarised in the formula (C)V(C). As regards the intensity (stress) accent, it occupied a fixed position, located on the penultimate syllable. In what follows we shall deal with the postulated consonants, presenting them in series, with the cognates that support their reconstruction.
